analysis.one_liner: Caps the manufacturer price of insulin at $20 per 1,000 units.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2023, sent to the Senate health committee, and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for drug companies to charge more than $20 per 1,000 units of insulin in the United States, however the insulin is packaged (vials, pens, or cartridges). It was introduced by Senator Bernie Sanders and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which never scheduled it for a vote. It died in committee when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use insulin, including the roughly 8 million Americans who depend on it to survive. Anyone paying the full list price at the pharmacy, or high costs through a deductible, would see the manufacturer's price for insulin cut sharply, since the largest manufacturers have charged far more than $20 per 1,000 units for decades.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a hard legal ceiling: manufacturers may not charge more than $20 per 1,000 units of insulin, regardless of vial, pen, or cartridge size.
The cap applies to all insulin licensed under the Public Health Service Act and still being marketed, including biosimilar versions.

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and Sanofi dominate the U.S. market) would bear the cost, giving up a large share of the revenue they currently earn from prices well above $20 per 1,000 units.

drawbacks.text: The cap applies to the price manufacturers charge, not the price patients pay at the pharmacy counter. Middlemen like pharmacy benefit managers and insurers sit between the manufacturer and the patient, so savings only reach patients fully if they are passed through.

A hard government price ceiling on a product where three companies dominate the market could reduce manufacturers' incentive to develop new insulin formulations or to keep older versions widely supplied at the capped price, an objection an honest supporter would have to answer. The bill text contains no supply obligation or fallback if manufacturers stop offering a product.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who use insulin, the upside is large and immediate: a legal ceiling on what manufacturers can charge for a drug discovered a century ago and cheap to produce. The main weakness is design: the cap controls the manufacturer price but not the final price patients pay, so its real-world benefit depends on middlemen passing savings along. It is a strong bill for patients whose main flaw is that it does not reach all the way to the pharmacy counter.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, which never scheduled it for a vote, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on March 9, 2023, joined by Senators Merkley and Markey as original cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Five Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The committee took no further action on the bill, and no vote was ever held in the Senate or the House before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers are better off, because they keep charging prices above the $20 cap the bill would have imposed. The committee's inaction also spared pharmacies' and insurers' supply chains any forced change. The committee that let it sit was chaired by the bill's own sponsor, Senator Sanders, who never scheduled it for a markup during the two-year Congress.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator (sponsor); Chairman, Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap insulin manufacturer prices at $20 per 1,000 units; as the HELP Committee chairman whose panel received the bill, never scheduled it for a markup or vote during the two-year Congress.

for.name: Jeff Merkley and Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; all six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and no Republican cosponsored.

industries.industry: Insulin manufacturers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi)
industries.note: The bill would cap what they can charge for insulin at $20 per 1,000 units, far below current list prices, cutting deeply into their insulin revenue. Their interest in the bill's failure ran against patients who pay those prices.

The bill does not regulate what middlemen and insurers charge or cover, only the manufacturer price, so their role and margins are left untouched. That gap means savings may not fully reach patients at the pharmacy counter.
